item.title: My Experience at the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos
item.dc:creator: Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé
item.description:
Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé on his experience at the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026.

The post My Experience at the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026.

When I got the email that I was selected for the Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop in Lagos, I knew, without doubt, that the cohort of writers I would engage with would be some of the finest around. I was not disappointed. The workshop put me in the same room with extremely talented writers I had read and admired from a distance. Some of us have shared publication credits and honours on longlists and shortlists of literary prizes over the past couple of years.

For two days, we were guests of the British Council and students at the feet of our primary facilitator, Nigerian writer, journalist, and editor, Molara Wood. Liberian-American writer Wayétu Moore also facilitated a session, and a publishing masterclass was held by Anwuli Ojogwu and Eghosa Imasuen of Narrative Landscape Press. 

The twelve selected writers for the workshop are Azeeza Adeowu, Chinenye Okechukwu, Ahmad Adedimeji Amobi, Chinonso Nzeh, Innocent Chizaram Ilo, Kingsley Alumona, Mayowa Fagbure, Mustapha Enesi, Oluwatobi Afolabi, Súnmisọ́lá Olúdé, Ufuoma Bakporhe, and Winifred Odunoku. A combination of writers who are also journalists, editors, filmmakers, among other things.

“Gotta Whack That Guy!”

I first encountered Molara Wood on social media, where she shared her commentary on a plethora of issues, from literature and culture to politics. So I particularly looked forward to learning from her. On the first day, when I walked into the workshop at the British Council, she was there, standing and already conversing with the writers present. 

By the time other writers arrived and the round of introductions began, it illuminated the sort of people I was in the room with. I had read the writing samples and excerpts recommended for reading ahead of the workshop. They were really good. These writers seemed assured in their craft, and it became further obvious as the conversations became robust.

Molara Wood, with all her brilliance, struck me even more with the animated manner in which she facilitated the workshop. As though she was more excited to teach than we were to be taught by her. This made the workshop flow seamlessly from the jump. We shared opinions on the assigned short stories. We discussed how well they used dialogue, descriptions, and language to reveal so much about the characters and the world they inhabit. We discussed how words, accents, and other idiosyncrasies of characters can reveal class, age and societal standing. This is why it is important for writers to observe the world. To observe the minute details of what makes up people, because these are the tools through which subtext can be created.

The arts are connected, especially through the basic principles of storytelling. Molara Wood recognised this by using the context of films, mostly classics, to highlight storytelling techniques for better understanding. We discussed the dangers of anachronism in contemporary fiction through the critique of a Nigerian novel and the anachronistic elements therein. 

She hammered on the importance of reading widely, beyond the mainstream, beyond the contemporary, across literary cultures and traditions. We must read widely so we can know exactly what we are writing in response to. 

The workshop’s goal is in its name. The rudiments of writing are well known to writers, but not so much those of editing. To polish a story to the best it can be. “To develop the inner practice of being attentive to define and understand the times”. Editing one’s own work can be difficult. The sentimental value we place on our words makes it hard to, as they say, “kill your darlings”, but it is a necessity for the beauty of a story to shine through. For the writing to be better, we simply “Gotta whack that guy!” as Molara Wood called out from her workshop material. 

The afternoon session was facilitated by the Liberian-American novelist, Wayétu Moore. Her session was on Speculative fiction/Magical Realism. Naturally, the question raised is the extent to which these categorisations apply to the works of those who write from cultures where the material and the mystical spheres are considered to be in constant interaction. Such that the happenings that seem magical to a Western mind are random stories one hears from neighbours, friends and family so often that they are as real as anything, and an immutable fact. Tales of cats that bring down house walls, of children who die and return again and again, of grandfathers who come back as babies, of birds dropping from the sky and transforming into old women. Wayétu Moore was in conversation with us about this. 

The most important eye-opener for me during this session was about plot and character building. The rules for writing nuanced characters are the same regardless of whether a story is speculative or realist. Writers tend to venerate certain characters as saints and demonise others with no redeemable qualities, such that they are a clear antithesis of the other. But human beings are not that way. A supposedly evil character can be a loving husband. A torturer can be a caring father when he returns home every night. This is the nature of humans, the nature of the characters we want to portray in stories. It has been said that reality doesn’t necessarily make sense, but fiction should.

The Caine Prize Self-Editing Workshop, held in Lagos on 17 and 18 November 2026.

“Forget technique… Write from here.”

We all had one question on our tongues on the second day of the workshop: who wrote the assigned anonymised short story we were to discuss? It was a shocking story, quality-wise, and was written by one of the greats of 20th-century African Writing, we came to find out. A story that meanders and pulls up new surprises with every line. In a workshop with a focus on editing, it was the perfect case study for our facilitator to have us note not only its obvious flaws, but also its strengths.

We learned even more about dialogue and voice, structural and contextual editing. The field was covered. Molara Wood wanted to get as much as possible done despite the short time we had together for the workshop. So we had to eat into our lunch breaks, quite literally. No complaints; there was so much to converse about. 

The sessions were interactive. We discussed each other’s writing samples, and then our works-in-progress in pairs, giving feedback on what we thought worked well, what didn’t. A way of putting into practice what we had spent hours learning during the workshop. One that was soon reaching its end. 

When Eghosa Imasuen and Anwuli Ojogwu of Narrative Landscape Press filled the room with their presence for the afternoon session, I knew it was going to be enjoyable. Eghosa Imasuen is a very jovial man, mixing English with Pidgin to land a point and make jokes. It felt as if he knew us all beforehand. 

The publishing industry in Nigeria has always fascinated me. What are contracts like? How well do books sell? These things are often shrouded in mystery. Eghosa spearheaded the session. Anwuli made her points where she thought necessary. Understanding the publishing process within a Nigerian publishing house like NLP was necessary for writers who, after fine-tuning stories or a novel, would seek out publishers. 

The session included tips on how to put together a publisher’s query for a manuscript, and the fine margins that can make a query sound professional and confident. “Be simple. Less is more,” Anwuli noted. You write a good story, rewrite, revise, edit, put together a pack of publishers’ queries and send it off with a hail of prayers. 

“Writers are the suppliers of stories,” Eghosa Imasuen explained. Publishers produce and sell them. It is looking at stories in the business sense, because publishing is a business, a precarious, courageous one. This was further highlighted when we got into the numbers of it all, information that I was glad to be privy to. The nature of publishing contracts, negotiations, typical first prints, marketing, royalties, publishers’ accounts and others. 

I don’t think there is a gathering of writers, particularly African writers nowadays, where the spectre of AI accusations hanging over any writer who wins a prize is not discussed. And surely, this conversation was had. We spoke about measures writers could take to avoid pitfalls, and to prove the human authorship of their work. Keep every single draft you make? Email them to friends? Record yourself writing? I reckon that no matter what one does in good faith, the bad actors who have adopted the AI boogeyman to hound an unlucky prize-winning African writer will not care. 

And maybe it is not only about AI, but also about sustained tropes in African literature, about formulaic ways of writing. It is ironic that in a workshop about the complexities and technicalities of craft, I was particularly struck by the words repeated like a refrain by Eghosa Imasuen when he addressed the issue. “Forget technique… write from here,” he said, pointing to his chest. I understood this as simply saying that since formulaic ways of writing are now easily replicated,  perhaps one should take a step back and just write as it comes from the heart.

By the end of the workshop, so many revelations had been made. I would never be the same writer I was when I first walked into that room. There was a networking event that evening attended by Donna McGowan, the Country Director at the British Council; Harry Keseina, Head of Arts and Culture at the British Council; Ajoke Bodunde of The Caine Prize; and other guests. There was more food and drinks. We listened to readings by fellow writers in such an amazing cohort. There were extra conversations and laughter.

Writing is a solitary act. Everything else afterwards is not. Being in the midst of other brilliant writers can create a sense of belonging. A feeling that there is a community to cheer for that can cheer you back. To remind you of the strengths and weaknesses you would not have otherwise noticed. To remind you that, indeed, despite the many layers of the technicalities of craft, all it really takes, most importantly, is to first write from the heart.

item.content:encoded:
The 11th edition of The Beatz Awards, held on Saturday, November 21, 2026, at the Shell Hall, MUSON Centre, Onikan, Lagos, was a remarkable celebration of music, creativity, excellence and the exceptional talents working behind the scenes of the Nigerian music industry.

Under the theme “Behind the Beat, Beyond the Beat,” this year’s ceremony brought together music professionals, industry stakeholders, producers, songwriters, DJs, engineers, media personalities and other key players to celebrate the creative minds whose contributions continue to shape the sound and business of African music.

Soso Soberekon Receives Special Recognition Award

One of the major highlights of the evening was the presentation of the Special Recognition Award to renowned music executive and industry figure, Soso Soberekon, in recognition of his remarkable contributions to the Nigerian music industry.

From talent discovery and artist development to music promotion, business development and industry connections, Soso Soberekon’s influence and commitment to the growth of Nigerian entertainment continue to resonate across different sectors of the culture.

The special recognition celebrates his role in creating opportunities, supporting talents and contributing to the development of the Nigerian music ecosystem.

May D and Shiiro Deliver Electrifying Performances

The ceremony also featured captivating musical performances, with award-winning singer May D delivering an electrifying performance that got the audience on their feet, while producer and songwriter Shiiro equally thrilled guests with an impressive performance, showcasing the creativity and musical excellence that The Beatz Awards continues to celebrate.

Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge: Kevwe Praise Emerges Winner

Another major highlight of the 11th edition was the highly anticipated Beatz to Banger Producers’ Challenge, an initiative designed to discover, nurture and provide opportunities for emerging music producers.

The competition provided a platform for talented producers who participated in the Beatz to Banger 2.0 training programme to showcase their creativity, technical abilities and music production skills before an audience of industry professionals.

Following an intense competition among the final five contestants, Kevwe Praise emerged as the ultimate winner, earning the coveted title and a cash prize of ₦1.5 million.

The winner’s cash cheque was presented by Princess Damilola Sonayon-James, APC Deputy Governorship Aspirant, alongside the Chief Executive Officer of The Beatz Awards, Elijah John.

The moment marked a significant milestone for the winning producer and reinforced The Beatz Awards’ commitment to creating tangible opportunities for emerging talents beyond recognition and celebration.

Through the Beatz to Banger initiative, the platform continues to bridge the gap between music education, talent discovery and industry opportunities, empowering the next generation of music producers to move from raw talent to industry readiness.

THE BEATZ AWARDS 2026 WINNERS

The following individuals and organisations emerged as winners across the various categories:

Music Production Categories

  • Afro Pop Producer of the Year – Jhay2unez
  • Afro Beat Producer of the Year – SBThaProducer
  • Afro R&B Producer of the Year – IBKSleek
  • Afro Hip-Hop Producer of the Year – JJay
  • Afro Highlife Producer of the Year – AykBeats
  • Afro Soul Producer of the Year – Niphkeys
  • Afro Dancehall Producer of the Year – Vtek
  • Afro Gospel Producer of the Year – Hunkie Beats
  • Female Producer of the Year – Loc The Plug
  • Male Producer of the Year – AykBeats
  • New Discovery Producer of the Year – JJay

Technical and Creative Categories

  • Mixing & Mastering Engineer of the Year – Millamix
  • Music Video Director of the Year – Jyde Ajala
  • Songwriter of the Year – Fola

Media and Entertainment Categories

  • Radio Station of the Year – Inspiration FM
  • Entertainment Station Award (Terrestrial) of the Year – Superscreen
  • Entertainment Station Award (Cable) of the Year – Trace Naija
  • DJ Male of the Year – DJ YK Mule
  • DJ Female of the Year – Dope Caesar
  • OAP of the Year – Cera
  • Blog of the Year – BellaNaija
  • Online Music Platform of the Year – Spotify

Music Business and Industry Categories

  • Artist Manager of the Year – Priest (Silent Lion)
  • Record Label of the Year – Dangbana Republic
  • Live Band of the Year – Cool Ice Band
  • A&R Category of the Year – Eskor Umo
  • Entertainment Lawyer of the Year – Oyinkansola “Foza” Fawehinmi

Special Recognition Award

  • Soso Soberekon

Eleven Years of Celebrating the Creators Behind the Sound

If your next braid appointment has you thinking beyond the usual ponytail or bun, Temi Nkem has an idea you might want to take to your hairstylist. The Big Brother Naija 2026 winner wore her thick braids in a high, sculptural updo, with oversized loops arranged into a crown. She paired it with a gold-and-black look, complete with metallic beauty details and contrasting textures.

Rather than letting her thick braids fall down her back, Temi has gathered them into a sleek, high updo, building them into an oversized crown of interlocking loops. The result is sculptural, full of volume and beautifully structured. It’s also a great example of how to style thick braids when you want a fresh way to wear them for an event. Pulling the hair up keeps the face open, while the loops create plenty of interest around the crown. And with the base kept sleek, the hairstyle gets to take centre stage without feeling too busy.

Temi Nkem accents her sleek looped braid updo with metallic gold-leaf detailing, brow crystal, and glossy nude lips.

Then there are the beauty details. Temi goes for smoky brown eyeshadow, full lashes and a glossy nude lip outlined in brown, keeping the makeup warm and complementary to the outfit. A little gold takes things further: there’s a tiny cross-shaped crystal between her brows, three vertical micro-beads on her chin, hammered circular gold earrings and flecks of metallic gold leaf tracing the side of her face, from her left temple down to her collarbone. It’s an unexpected beauty detail, and one that ties in beautifully with the colours of her outfit.

Temi Nkem shows how to style thick braids into a sculptural crown paired with a gold-and-black corset gown.

Now, about that gown! Temi shows how to wear gold and black with ease, starting with a structured matte-gold leather corset bodice. It features vertical seam boning, a deep V-plunge neckline and a sharply defined V-shaped basque waist. Below it, a fitted black velvet skirt brings a different texture into the look, while matching off-the-shoulder velvet arm bands complete the silhouette. The contrast between the gold leather and plush black velvet is what makes the combination work so well. Rather than having both colours compete for attention, the matte gold adds warmth and the black velvet gives the outfit balance.

So, if thick braids are next on your salon mood board, you might want to save Temi’s updo. And if you’re planning a gold-and-black outfit, her mix of leather and velvet is another styling idea worth keeping.

item.title: Enoch Adeagbo Was Denied Admission for Being Too Young. At 19, He’s Set to Graduate with First-Class Honours
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.description:
Written by Enoch Adeagbo.

The post Enoch Adeagbo Was Denied Admission for Being Too Young. At 19, He’s Set to Graduate with First-Class Honours appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
My name is Enoch Adeagbo. In 2021, at the age of 14, I was refused admission because I was too young. I was very sad because the reason had nothing to do with my academic ability. My parents encouraged me to apply to another university, and I eventually gained admission to Ajayi Crowther University (ACU), Oyo, at the age of 14.

On Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at 19, I will graduate from ACU with First Class Honours in Civil Engineering, having earned a CGPA of 4.79 out of 5.00, as the second-best student in my department and the third-best student in the Faculty of Engineering.

If I had given up and not applied to another school, I might not be here today sharing my journey.

Where it all began

As a child, I often accompanied my father to construction sites. I enjoyed watching structures take shape from foundation stage to completion. My interest in how buildings were designed and constructed gradually developed into a desire to become an engineer.

At 14, however, I was considerably younger than most of my course mates. People frequently reminded me of my age, and I had to adjust. I learnt to focus on my studies, take part in university activities and make the most of the opportunity I had been given.

In the 2022/2023 session, at 15, I received the Overall Best Student in Engineering of the Year award at the 200-level. I had not expected it, but it was also an encouraging recognition of my work, and it motivated me to stay consistent.

The C that taught me something

But being interested in a course does not necessarily mean you’d understand it completely. I learnt this in the first semester of 400 level, when I got a C in Structural Analysis, a three-unit course I thought I understood. I was surprised because I had been confident in my knowledge of the course.

That experience made me reflect on my approach to studying. I became more deliberate about understanding concepts rather than simply assuming I had mastered them. Studying with a group and teaching my coursemates also became valuable. Explaining a topic to someone else also helped me understand the course more.

More than lectures

Beyond the classroom, I served as the Academic Officer of the Nigerian Universities Engineering Students’ Association (NUESA), ACU Chapter, for the 2025/2026 session. I also served as an Assistant Class Representative and was involved in chapel activities as a chapel worker. 

My faith in God has played an important role throughout my university journey. It shaped my discipline, decisions and priorities, and helped me remain intentional about my responsibilities.

I am grateful to my parents, who made sure I did not have to worry about finances while pursuing my education. Their support allowed me to concentrate on my studies and other responsibilities without the additional burden of financial concerns.

Learning on real construction sites

My engineering education has also involved practical experiences outside the university.

In 2023, during my internship at T.E.A.M. (Nigeria) Limited, I was exposed to engineering consultancy in the construction of Obafemi Awolowo railway infrastructure in Ibadan. In 2024, I worked on drainage construction at LIDAMYT Global Contracting Services.

I subsequently completed a six-month structural design internship in 2025 at Basit Opeloyeru and Associates, where I worked on structural modelling, analysis, design and detailing, alongside exposure to construction projects through site visits.

Since July 2026, I have been working as an Engineering Intern at GLIC, gaining further practical experience on five-storey and seven-storey reinforced concrete buildings. My responsibilities have included supervising aspects of construction such as ribbed slab works, shear walls, staircases and roof structures.

Initially, I felt inexperienced when I was given on-site supervisory responsibilities, and instructing older artisans. However, as I became more experienced with construction processes and gained practical exposure, my confidence gradually improved. The experience has helped me understand the responsibility involved in ensuring that construction activities follow engineering drawings and specifications.

What comes next

I hope to pursue postgraduate studies abroad through a scholarship opportunity. My ambition is to continue developing in structural engineering while also exploring research and professional opportunities in water resources engineering. I hope to build a career that combines professional practice, research and meaningful contributions to infrastructure and environmental development.

I am grateful to my project supervisor, Engr. Dr A.T. Adeyokunnu, as well as the lecturers and friends who contributed to my university experience.

To anyone who has been told they are too young, too early or not ready, a setback does not have to determine how your story ends. Mine did not. I was eventually given an opportunity, and I made the most of it.

Debo has officially joined the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts (RSA), a UK-based institution recognised globally for bringing together changemakers across the arts, social innovation and public life.

item.content:encoded:
The Design Table 2026 brought together some of the voices, ideas and creative forces shaping African fashion for an afternoon of industry exchange, recognition and conversation. The annual cultural platform, produced by So.Me Solutions, welcomed designers, fashion entrepreneurs, industry leaders, media personalities and fashion enthusiasts for its latest edition.

Held at GRAS Lagos, Victoria Island, during Lagos Fashion Week, this year’s gathering explored the people, perspectives and opportunities influencing the future of African fashion. The event also marked a significant milestone for So.Me Solutions, which celebrates 10 years as a 360 communications agency.

Among the guests were Folake Amber (Tiffany Amber), Bola Balogun (Glam Brand), Sharon Adeleke, Beverly Naya, Awed by Moni, Marvy Olugu (House of Marvee) and Funmi Ford, alongside other familiar faces from across fashion, entertainment and the creative scene.

A Seat at the Table for the Next Generation

A major highlight of this year’s edition was the Next Gen Design Impact Award, which received 101 applications from emerging designers. Following the selection process, three finalists, Sultana, Dimeji Ilori and Bjuv Woman, were shortlisted for the award.

The finalists were evaluated by a five-member jury comprising Dr. Yetty Ogunnubi, Odio Mimonet, Eniafe Momodu, Ugonna-Ora Owoh and Yoanna “Pepper”, with guests also participating in the voting process.

Bhuv Woman emerged as the winner, receiving the $5,000 grand prize funded by Vlisco, Patrón and Culture Lab. In addition, Odio Mimonet extended a further $2,000 in award support, bringing the total prize support associated with the award to $7,000.
Beyond the financial support, the winning package includes mentorship, industry access and opportunities to further advance the designer’s work. The announcement was an emotional moment for Bhuv Woman, who was visibly moved as she received the recognition and expressed gratitude to the organisers.
Through the award, The Design Table continues to create opportunities for emerging designers to gain visibility, access and recognition while connecting them with established voices and resources within the fashion industry.

Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion?

The conversations continued with a speakers session titled “Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion?”, moderated by Yvan Otu and featured Mai Atafo, founder of ATAFO; Ezinne Chinkata, founder of Zinkata; Sacha Okoh, fashion entrepreneur and creative director of Viva; Kiki Osinbajo, founder of CIAR; and Tess Tanaka, founder of Moda54.

The session explored how African fashion can move beyond being treated as a niche category and become more firmly integrated into the wider global fashion landscape. Discussions touched on what it takes for African brands to be stocked, worn and embraced as part of everyday fashion, alongside the realities of production, pricing, distribution, customer experience and access to markets.


The conversation reinforced the importance of building a fashion ecosystem where creative talent is supported by the structures, opportunities and industry connections needed for sustainable growth.

A Decade of So.Me Solutions and the Vision Behind The Design Table

This year’s edition also carried special significance for So.Me Solutions, marking 10 years of the agency’s work in communications. Founded by Elizabeth Osho, So.Me Solutions is a 360 communications agency working across brand communications and the creative industries.

The Design Table reflects Liz Osho’s vision of creating meaningful platforms that bring people together, encourage important conversations and contribute to the growth of industries and communities. Over the years, the platform has become a space for industry voices to connect, exchange ideas and recognise the people contributing to the evolution of African fashion.
Through this platform, So.Me Solutions continues to create opportunities for connection, collaboration and conversations that contribute to the growth of the creative industry.

 

Sponsors, Partners and Supporters

A special thank you to our sponsors, @vlisco, @culturelab.africa, @themofa54, @patron and @yvesrochernigeria, for helping make this year’s edition possible.

We also appreciate our partners, including GRAS Lagos, Mikano Motors, Blue Poppy and Jacque, for their support in bringing the experience to life.

Our media partners included FashionEVO, Style Vitae, Lhaude Africa, BellaNaija, The Will Downtown and Guzang.

As The Design Table looks ahead, its continued focus remains on creating room for meaningful conversations, celebrating emerging talent and strengthening the connections that move African fashion forward.

For more information and updates, follow @thedesigntablehq and @somesolutionsco.

item.content:encoded:
Danielle Adewusi displays the sweeping circular halo backpiece and floor-length beaded train of her Benin-inspired national costume.

A little Benin royalty on the Miss Universe stage? Danielle Adewusi is bringing it to Puerto Rico. For the 75th edition of the competition in San Juan, Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 has arrived at the National Costume runway with Daughter of the Coral Throne, an Edo-inspired creation that brings the history of the ancient Benin Kingdom into the spotlight. And in case you missed that detail, Danielle designed the entire look herself.

Now, where do we begin with this costume? The red coral beads are everywhere, from the sheer-panelled corset bodysuit and its sweetheart neckline, trimmed with gold-toned cowrie shells, to the floor-sweeping beaded overskirt and train. Look a little closer and there’s a miniature Queen Idia mask emblem at the hip.

Danielle Adewusi holds her gold ceremonial staff diagonally across Daughter of the Coral Throne against a waterside garden backdrop.

Then comes the fan-shaped coral bead headpiece, followed by a sweeping circular halo backpiece with cascading bead fringes. A tall gold ceremonial staff, topped with a sculpted Queen Idia mask, completes the look. Sculpted bronze-gold motifs and thousands of beads bring the whole tribute together, with each detail drawing from the artistry and royal traditions of the Benin Kingdom.

Danielle Adewusi pairs warm bronzed makeup and sleek cornrows with red coral beadwork and gold cowrie detailing.

Of course, Danielle isn’t leaving us to admire the costume without knowing what inspired it. She shared the story behind Daughter of the Coral Throne, explaining how she wanted to honour her Edo heritage and celebrate a kingdom whose history and identity remain, even after many of its treasures were taken:

For my Miss Universe National Costume, I honour my Edo heritage and the extraordinary legacy of the ancient Kingdom of Benin, one of Africa’s greatest civilisations… Daughter of the Coral Throne reimagines the splendour of Edo royalty through contemporary African couture. Thousands of coral-inspired beads celebrate the prestige and authority of Benin royalty, while gold detailing pays tribute to the kingdom’s master craftsmen. The circular backpiece symbolises the continuity of our ancestry, radiating across generations. In my hand, a golden ceremonial staff honours the Oba of Benin, representing leadership, royal authority and an unbroken lineage.

And as I follow in my mother’s footsteps, 35 years after she wore the Miss Universe Nigeria crown, I am reminded that legacy is not simply inherited. It is preserved, honoured and carried forward.

Danielle Adewusi honours her Edo heritage in Daughter of the Coral Throne ahead of the Miss Universe 2026 finale

There’s a personal connection to this Miss Universe journey, too. Danielle, a 29-year-old Lagos-born medical doctor and King’s College London graduate, won Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 in September, following in the footsteps of her mother, Tonia Okogbenin, who represented Nigeria at the competition in 1991.

She’s also pursuing her medical career and her women’s health initiative, Scrub the Stigma. Now, she’s carrying that family history with her as she joins 116 contestants from around the world, including 17 African queens, ahead of the grand finale, tomorrow, 24 November, in Puerto Rico.

item.content:encoded:
Structural tailoring meets monochrome colour play in Mercy Aigbe’s olive and sage green asoebi look.

Whenever a green dress code lands in your inbox for an upcoming wedding or celebration, the goal is always making the colour feel fresh and flattering rather than predictable. Nollywood star and filmmaker, Mercy Aigbe just gave us the sweetest blueprint for how to wear green lace for asoebi without letting heavy fabric wear you.

The secret to nailing monochrome green for asoebi is mixing your shades and textures so you avoid one flat block of colour from head to toe. Mercy’s gown pairs a smooth, velvety olive corset—complete with visible boning and a central trail of beaded leaf appliqués—with a heavily beaded mermaid skirt in the same olive family.

Mercy Aigbe showcases the full silhouette of her olive green corset and beaded lace mermaid gown paired with a marbled sage headtie.

Keeping the bodice matte while the skirt sparkles lets the silhouette breathe, and crowning the outfit with a lighter, marbled sage headtie (gele) brightens up the face far better than a dark green wrap ever could. When taking your own green lace to the tailor, borrow her structural tricks: an asymmetrical off-the-shoulder neckline with 3D floral cutouts draws the eye upward, while a diagonal beaded sash-peplum along one hip creates curves without adding bulk around your waist.

Mercy Aigbe pairs her olive green lace outfit with a deep red crystal crescent clutch and matching red manicure.

As for how to accessorise a green monochrome outfit, skip the usual all-gold default and bring in a rich contrast colour. Olive and sage sit right opposite red on the colour wheel, which is why Mercy’s gold jewellery set with dark red stones, crescent red crystal clutch, and glossy red nails pop so well against the green. Paired with warm golden-bronze eyeshadow and a glossy nude-brown lip, the whole look feels balanced, celebratory, and ready for any guest list.

item.content:encoded:
Official Unveiling of Temi Nkem and Karan Checker

Temi Nkem (born Temitope Chigbue), ultimate finalist of Big Brother  Naija Show Ya Sef, the eleventh edition of Africa’s TV game show, added another feather to her cap just weeks after coming out tops  at the eleventh edition of the DStv reality show.  

Checkers Custard, Nigeria’s custard brand, welcomed the starlet as chief brand influencer cum Brand Ambassador at a signing ceremony chaired by Karan Checker, Managing Director, Checkers Africa, at a ceremony witnessed by the media, friends, staff,  influencers and a host of well-wishers. 

It’s a Homecoming!  

Karan Checker, Temi Nkem and Ashish Checker

The entire continent of Africa witnessed the 21-year-old influencer’s  genuine love for Checkers Custard during her ten-week stay in Big  Brother’s house with the incessant trips to the kitchen primarily to make  her favourite snack, in-between meal filler and as a whole meal with  select pairings. Checkers Custard was central to her nutritional routine. 

File signing

Temi came home. Temi Nkem x Checkers Custard  

Temi, at the winning prize presentation a few days after the grand finale, remarked, 

“…we use Checkers Custard for our cake and custard in London. When I  was telling everybody cake and custard is dessert, they were saying no,  it’s breakfast, so I tried it the first time… it was ‘bussing’… I don’t know  how to cook… but that one I needed to make sure I made sure I knew  how to do, and I am so happy, so grateful”

The British-born Nigerian Accounting & Finance undergrad came into the country solely to participate in the fiercely contested game show and excelled week in, week out, showing her prowess in executing a strategy of being herself, showing her resilience and goodly disposition. 

These traits did not go unnoticed as Checkers Custard’s brand handlers watched keenly, finally determining to welcome home their providence-chosen brand evangelist. 

A Truly Natural Fit  

Keran Checker, the Managing Director of Checkers Africa Limited, the  parent company of Checkers Custard, at the signing ceremony in his  speech said,  

“Temi Nkem is one of a kind; she came, she saw, and conquered the world with her charm and exceptional attitude at Big Brother Naija, and this made us take a deep look into the beautiful and interesting young lady and explore the potential of her representing the brand due to shared values and unparalleled natural alignment”. 

While noting that not every Checkers Custard lover in Big Brother’s house  in the future would automatically merit an ambassadorial appointment  with Checkers Custard, and what made Ms. Chigbue different, Head of  Marketing, Checkers Africa, Timothy Ogundele said in his closing  remarks on her character traits, 

“Even with a fiery personality and unapologetic, Temi remained true to  her values demonstrating a deep sense of restraint and discipline making  her suitable for our brand.” 

A Date with Temi Nkem  

The official signing ceremony event took place at the offices of Checkers  Africa, playing host to the media, content creators, and friends interacting and networking over ample food and drinks and good music.  

Temi & Karan Checker

Honouring her multiple roots, Temi arrived to Ayanjo Dance Troupe performing a Delta dance routine. Upon her ascending to the event floor after the meet and greet, she was welcomed with enrapturing Yoruba praise poetry by the renowned Ayodele Tayelolu Deborah (also known as TK Voices Akewi) before proceeding to the conference room where the media parley unfolded. 

There was a short presentation, an edited recap of numerous clips of  Temi Nkem in the Big Brother house making Checkers Custard, an emotional throwback showcasing her affection for the brand before the signing and cake-cutting. 

During the Q&A session after the signing ceremony, Temi was probed by  a cross-section of the press on whether her actions in the house were pre-planned or  a script; and Temi responded accordingly,

item.title: Ghana’s Black Challenge Conquer the World With First-Ever Amputee Football World Cup Title
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija.com
item.description:
Ghana’s Black Challenge defeated Morocco 1–0 in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico, to claim their first-ever WAFF Amputee Football World Cup title, with captain Richard Arthur Opentil scoring the winner and Mubarik Mohammed winning the Golden Boot.

The post Ghana’s Black Challenge Conquer the World With First-Ever Amputee Football World Cup Title appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today!.
item.content:encoded:
Pure joy on the pitch as Ghana’s Black Challenge mark their historic 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup triumph in Mexico.

Ghana’s national amputee football team, the Black Challenge, have officially conquered the world after edging Morocco 1–0 in the final of the 2026 World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF) World Cup in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico on Sunday, November 22, 2026. For anyone keeping an eye on international football and West African sporting milestones, this is a moment worth celebrating—it marks Ghana’s very first Amputee Football World Cup crown.

The championship match brought together two African powerhouses and served as a high-stakes showdown between familiar rivals, following Ghana’s earlier continental triumphs against Morocco, including the 2024 African Amputee Cup of Nations final. Captain Richard Arthur Opentil stepped up as the decisive hero, scoring the lone goal in the 32nd minute. From there, Ghana dug deep with grit, smart positioning, and defensive discipline to shut out Morocco and bring the trophy home.

Intense action between Morocco and Ghana during the 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico.

What makes Ghana’s run in Mexico even more memorable is how much they had to overcome in the knockout stages. The Black Challenge defeated the United States 3–1 in the Round of 16, eased past Egypt 2–0 in the quarter-finals behind a brace from forward Mubarik Mohammed, and then edged a tense semi-final 1–1 after extra time before winning 4–3 on penalties.

Individual brilliance shone right alongside the team trophy. Forward Mubarik Mohammed finished as the tournament’s top scorer with seven goals, earning the Golden Boot award. Back home, the achievement sparked widespread celebration, with congratulatory messages from Ghana’s leadership—including President John Dramani Mahama and the Ministry of Sports and Recreation—alongside financial backing and pledges from corporate supporters and philanthropists such as Gold Fields Ghana and Mohammed Raii through the EEZZY Group Foundation. Speaking after the victory, captain Richard Arthur Opentil dedicated the triumph to Ghana and its supporters as an early Christmas gift to the nation.

Ghana’s Black Challenge celebrate lifting their maiden 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup trophy in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico.

If you are wondering what the WAFF Amputee Football World Cup is all about, it is the premier international championship for amputee football, governed globally by the World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF). Played according to rules adapted from FIFA’s Laws of the Game, amputee football is fast-paced, physically demanding, and thrilling to watch.

Matches feature seven players per side—outfield players with lower-limb amputations playing on forearm crutches without prostheses, and goalkeepers with single-arm amputations—with crutches treated as part of the player’s body rather than a tool to intentionally play the ball.

Sometimes trying to do a good deed for someone else is how everything goes sideways. Mercy Johnson–Okojie, Jim Iyke and Lilian Esoro carry the story forward under Kayode Kasum‘s direction, working from a screenplay by Folasade Osibo and with Joy Grant–Ekong and Solate Ovundah–Akarolo on board as producers.

Tolu LordTanner directs this suspenseful drama starring Godspower Nwogwugwu, Damilola Onitilo, Oyeyemi Adeoye and Ovy Godwin.

item.content:encoded:
For many people, buying property is one of the biggest financial decisions they will ever make. Yet, knowing who to trust, how to verify ownership and whether a property is worth the investment can make the process overwhelming.

It is a challenge Solape Fayemi hopes to address with the launch of Saina Properties, a real estate company now operating across Nigeria, the United Kingdom, the United States and the United Arab Emirates.

Officially unveiled at an event held on 17 November at the Marriott Hotel, Ikeja GRA, Lagos, Saina Properties is built around a simple idea: property ownership should be guided by sound advice, proper verification and professional support, not just the excitement of closing a deal.

For Solape, whose experience in the investment industry shaped her understanding of money, risk and wealth creation, the decision to establish the company came from recognising the need for a more considered approach to real estate.

“We are not building Saina Properties because the world needs another company selling properties. We are building Saina because we believe there is room for a different kind of real estate experience. One where advice comes before the transaction, where due diligence is not treated as an inconvenience, and where people are encouraged to ask questions, understand their options and make informed decisions,” she said at the launch.


That philosophy is reflected in the company’s three core areas of expertise: Advisory & Verification, Sales & Brokerage, and Developments. Rather than focusing solely on connecting buyers to properties, Saina brings together the guidance investors need to assess opportunities, the support required to navigate property transactions, and involvement in real estate development.

The company is also building on experience gained before its official launch, having supported more than 25 clients with property opportunities across different markets.

An important part of its proposition is the role of professional expertise in protecting property investors. Fayemi’s position raises a familiar question: people consult doctors for medical concerns and lawyers for legal matters, so why do some investors leave significant property decisions in the hands of relatives simply because they are available or familiar with the location?

While trust and family relationships matter, they do not automatically translate into the technical knowledge needed to assess a property, verify its documentation or understand its investment potential. These decisions require proper checks, market understanding and accountability.

With its operations spanning four markets, Saina Properties aims to support individuals and investors looking to navigate property ownership with greater clarity, whether they are buying, selling or exploring development opportunities.

Its guiding promise captures the thinking behind the business: “With Saina Properties, you own with certainty.”


Solape Fayemi is the Chief Executive Officer of Saina Properties, a real estate company operating across Nigeria, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the United Arab Emirates. She leads the company’s vision and strategic direction, overseeing its work across property advisory and verification, sales and brokerage, and developments. Drawing on her experience in the investment industry, Solape brings a strong understanding of wealth creation, risk management, and capital preservation to her approach to real estate.

Under her leadership, Saina Properties is focused on making property ownership a more informed and transparent experience, built on professional guidance, due diligence and long-term client relationships.

item.title: How Mary Akinwola Graduated with a Distinction from Oxford After Receiving Multiple Scholarships
item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.description:
My name is Mary Akinwola. I’m a physiotherapist, a strategy consultant, a healthcare entrepreneur, and I recently graduated from the University of Oxford with a distinction in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation. I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying […]

item.content:encoded:
Mary Akinwola graduated from the University of Oxford after receiving the Chevening and Mastercard Foundation Scholarships.

My name is Mary Akinwola. I’m a physiotherapist, a strategy consultant, a healthcare entrepreneur, and I recently graduated from the University of Oxford with a distinction in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation.

I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying it yet. Haha!

One thing about me is that I like to be involved. I am sometimes curious about things that have absolutely nothing to do with what I’m supposed to be doing, and I genuinely enjoy working with people. I like organising things, bringing people together, and seeing an idea move forward to get accomplished. So I have known that going to Oxford was never going to be just about getting a master’s degree.

Let me explain how I ended up there.

I studied Physiotherapy at the University of Ibadan, where I graduated with First-Class Honours. During my undergraduate years, I was involved in quite a lot outside academics: student leadership, journalism, research, community health programmes and advocacy.

My involvement in community health exposed me to how differently people experience healthcare depending on where they live, what they can afford and what information they have access to.

I loved being a physiotherapist, and that allowed me to interrogate questions that went beyond individual patient care. Why do some people receive good healthcare while others struggle to access even basic services? How do we make healthcare more affordable? What role can technology play? And why do some seemingly good healthcare programmes struggle to produce lasting change?

Eventually, I realised I wanted to study and work in a field that constantly seeks to improve health systems.

I researched different programmes across the US and UK, hoping to study at institutions that have international audiences where I could build a diverse perspective in health. I came across the MSc in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation at the University of Oxford’s Nuffield Department of Medicine. It aligned with many of my interests, so I applied.

I also needed a scholarship because, quite frankly, I couldn’t afford Oxford. It was a humbling and affirming process. I was awarded scholarships such as the Chevening Scholarship and two Oxford-based scholarships. I still feel fortunate to have received and chosen the Mastercard Foundation-Africa Oxford Initiative Scholarship, which fully funded my studies.

I am deeply grateful for that opportunity.

Now, I think it’s important to say that I was very excited about the academic programme. I wanted to understand healthcare systems better, learn new research methods and become more effective at designing and evaluating healthcare services.

However, I was also very excited about everything else. I was going to be at Oxford! There were going to be people from different countries, lectures, events, societies, research opportunities, interesting conversations, and all sorts of things I didn’t even know existed yet.

I wanted to experience as much of it as possible.

One of the first things I realised was how much to learn from other people. My classmates came from different professional and geographical backgrounds, and our conversations were often as interesting as the lectures themselves. 

Someone would describe how healthcare worked in their country, and I’d realise that something I had always assumed was normal was actually quite specific to my own experience. Or we’d discuss a health systems problem, and someone would approach it in a way I hadn’t considered.

I loved that. 

I also found the academic programme quite demanding when we were introduced to unfamiliar methods or theories. There were times when I had to sit with an idea for a while before it made sense, but I enjoyed being challenged, and I had wonderful classmates and teachers to learn from. The lectures and lecturers were very interactive and creative in their approach to imparting knowledge. I am still inspired by their methods and hope to collaborate with the program someday. 

Outside the classroom, I did what I usually do: I found things to get involved in.

I became Class Representative for my cohort, worked on consulting projects with the University of Oxford’s Making a Difference Program and the Oxford Strategy Group, joined the Skoll Centre Impact Lab, and attended the Skoll World Forum.

I participated in the BCG-Oxford Africa Case Competition, where my team emerged as first runner-up. I presented research at academic conferences, received a presentation prize, and helped lead an Innovation Seed Fund programme which supported 4 African teams with funding and readiness support.

Gleaning from the creative approach applied in my lectures, I also co-organised a simulation workshop marking the tenth anniversary of the Africa Oxford Initiative with some of my closest friends (Amina, Farida and Lydia).

Sometimes, I had several commitments happening around the same period, and I had to figure out how to make everything work. I had to up time management and I also learned to say no in many cases. 

I genuinely enjoyed everything I did. I wasn’t doing these things just to have something to put on my CV. I liked the people I was meeting, the problems we were trying to solve, and the opportunity to try my hand at different things. The funniest part is that, towards the end of the programme, my classmates and teaching staff voted me “Extracurricular Legend.” I laughed so much when I got up to collect the award. Apparently, I had developed a reputation for being involved in everything. Naija no dey carry last sha.

I think what made my time at Oxford special, though, was the people. I met some wonderfully brilliant, generous and interesting people. I had conversations that made me question things I’d always believed, and others that were just completely unserious. I built friendships that I really hope will last for years. I felt comfortable expressing myself, asking questions, trying new things and sometimes just admitting that I didn’t know something.

When you spend a lot of time working towards particular goals, it can be easy to think about your life in terms of what you need to achieve next. Get the degree. Secure the opportunity. Build the company. Make the next move.

I am still very ambitious, and I don’t think that’s going to change, but I also really enjoyed being where I was. I enjoyed learning simply because something was interesting. I enjoyed discovering new places, meeting people, spending time with my friends and participating in activities that had nothing to do with my career.

It felt like such a complete year, and then I graduated with a distinction!

I was so happy. I had worked hard academically, and it was wonderful to see that reflected in my results, but I was also proud that I had made so much of the wider experience.

Someone described Oxford as the most flower-like season, and I know that’s a slightly unusual description, but it really is how I feel. I bloomed, really.

My family has been happy about the graduation, and that means a lot to me. My mum is a physiotherapist, and she has been an enormous influence on my life. Growing up, I watched her work very hard to provide for my siblings and me and ensure we received a good education. She made considerable sacrifices, and I am very grateful to her.

I sometimes think about the little girl who followed her mum to work and spent hours reading whatever medical books she could find. I don’t think she would have predicted this particular chapter of her life.

I am grateful to the Mastercard Foundation, the Africa Oxford Initiative, my lecturers, my friends, St Peter’s College, my mentors and everyone who helped make my Oxford experience what it was.

I am excited about working with organisations that drive change, especially in healthcare and excited about Rehabify Health, the company I’m building to make rehabilitation and recovery care more accessible across Africa.

My experiences as a physiotherapist showed me how much people need appropriate support to recover from pain, injuries and other health conditions. Oxford helped me think more intellectually about how we could develop and evaluate better systems to deliver that care. I want to bring those experiences together and continue building solutions that make a difference.

I also want to keep doing the things that made my Oxford year so wonderful: remaining curious, trying new things, meeting people and making room for experiences I haven’t necessarily planned.

If there’s anything I would tell someone who is hoping to pursue an opportunity like this, it’s that you should absolutely do it and prepare well, but please, don’t become so consumed by the next achievement that you forget to enjoy the experiences you’re having along the way.

Make friends, ask questions, try something unfamiliar, be willing to change your mind and give yourself room to discover new things about who you are.

I don’t know exactly what the next few years will bring, but I’m excited to find out.

For now, I am very thankful​​ to God. Once again, I am Mary Akinwola, and I work on healthcare transformation, especially how we use technology and innovative delivery models to improve access, quality and affordability. I also lead Rehabify Health, where we are building solutions to scale rehabilitation across Africa. 

Oxford MSc. Distinction and, apparently, Extracurricular Legend. Not bad at all!

Diana Eneje and Pascal Godwin‘s forever journey has begun, but first of all, introductions! Three months after Pascal proposed against the backdrop of Cape Town’s mountains and vineyards in August 2026, the Nigerian fashion influencer and entrepreneur and her Lagos-based businessman fiancé have taken another lovely step towards walking down the aisle. While they are not married just yet, the couple have officially held their introduction ceremony, bringing both families together ahead of their traditional and white weddings.

For anyone unfamiliar with the tradition, the introduction is an important first step in many Nigerian weddings. It is when the couple’s families meet formally, exchange greetings, offer prayers and give their blessings as the relationship moves towards marriage. And while the main wedding celebrations are still ahead, Diana and Pascal have given us a first look at what we can expect from their wedding style.

item.content:encoded:
Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport.

What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me?

I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine.

First, Understand What You Are Booking

A layover is generally a connection between flights; a stopover is a longer, planned break in your journey. Airlines define these differently, and the distinction matters because some offer special hotel packages, sightseeing tours or complimentary accommodation to qualifying passengers.

For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer.

Turkish Airlines: Turn Istanbul Into Part of Your Holiday

Turkish Airlines operates a Stopover in Istanbul programme for eligible international passengers connecting through Istanbul Airport. For visa purposes, Nigerians do not qualify, but with a valid Turkish visa you would be able to qualify for some of the perks. 

Qualifying travellers with connections of at least 20 hours and up to seven days may receive complimentary hotel accommodation. Under the standard programme, eligible Economy Class passengers can receive one night in a four-star hotel, while Business Class passengers may receive two nights in a five-star or boutique hotel.

Imagine travelling from Abuja or Lagos through Istanbul to London, Paris or another European destination. Rather than treating Istanbul as somewhere you simply change planes, you could plan time to experience the Grand Bazaar, the Bosphorus and the city’s extraordinary cultural heritage. The programme has specific conditions, including qualifying return tickets, participating countries of departure and an application made at least 72 hours before the relevant flight.

The complimentary accommodation does not cover every expense. Airport transfers, visa fees and other personal costs remain your responsibility. And for Nigerian passport holders, permission to enter Türkiye must be established before departure. A hotel voucher is not a substitute for a visa. There is also Touristanbul, a separate complimentary sightseeing programme for eligible passengers with shorter connections, typically between six and 24 hours. The two programmes have different conditions and cannot simply be combined.

Qatar Airways: A Stopover That Requires More Planning

Qatar Airways offers an opportunity to turn a connection through Doha into an additional holiday. However, for Nigerian passport holders, there is an important distinction between the airline’s advertised stopover offers and the actual requirements for entering Qatar.

While Qatar Airways promotes discounted stopover accommodation, Nigerian travellers should not assume they can access these packages without first satisfying Qatar’s visa requirements. Under the arrangement applicable to Nigerian travellers, obtaining the relevant visa requires purchasing an eligible Discover Qatar package with a minimum of three nights’ accommodation from accredited travel companies in Nigeria.

This means the stopover is not necessarily an opportunity to enjoy complimentary or heavily discounted accommodation. Instead, its value lies in the possibility of incorporating Doha into an international journey without purchasing an entirely separate return flight from Nigeria. For example, if you are travelling from Lagos to Singapore through Doha, you could investigate a ticket that allows you to spend three nights in Qatar before continuing to Singapore.

You would still need to budget for the qualifying Discover Qatar accommodation package, visa requirements, meals, activities and other expenses. The potential saving is therefore in the flight arrangement rather than the hotel. This is an important lesson about stopover programmes: what an airline advertises globally may not be equally accessible to every passport holder. Before booking, confirm your visa eligibility, the required Discover Qatar package and whether the extended stopover changes your airfare.

Ethiopian Airlines: Discover Addis Ababa on Your Way to Another Destination

For travellers heading to destinations across Africa and beyond, Ethiopian Airlines offers an opportunity worth investigating.

Eligible passengers connecting through Addis Ababa for between eight and 24 hours on qualifying Ethiopian Airlines tickets can receive complimentary hotel accommodation, meals and airport transfers. The airline also offers sightseeing experiences through Ethiopian Holidays.

Imagine flying from Abuja to Cape Town through Addis Ababa. Instead of spending a long connection inside the airport, you could use an eligible stopover to experience Ethiopian coffee culture, local cuisine and some of the capital’s attractions before continuing to South Africa.

The airline generally issues accommodation vouchers to qualifying passengers at their departure airport or transit desk (but make sure you already have your visa before going to the desk).

Passengers wishing to leave the airport must still satisfy Ethiopia’s entry requirements. The airline may assist with transit documentation under its qualifying programme, but this should be confirmed before travel. For me, this is an excellent example of how a journey through Africa can become an opportunity to discover more of the continent.

Emirates: Understand the Difference Between Dubai Connect and a Dubai Holiday

Dubai is already a familiar destination to many Nigerian travellers, but there is an important distinction between deliberately stopping in Dubai and qualifying for Emirates’ Dubai Connect service.

Dubai Connect can provide accommodation and other transit assistance to eligible passengers with qualifying connections, generally between six and 26 hours. However, it is designed around the best available flight connection, not simply a passenger’s desire to extend a holiday.

If you deliberately choose a much longer connection when a shorter eligible one exists, you may not qualify for the complimentary service. That does not mean you cannot plan Dubai into a wider holiday. You can investigate a paid multi-city itinerary or a ticket that allows a longer stay. UAE government is also constantly changing its rules, so make sure to check all this properly before booking that trip.

For example, you might arrange Lagos to Dubai, spend several nights there, then continue to Bangkok or Singapore before returning home. But that is a planned multi-city journey, not necessarily a free airline stopover. Understanding the difference prevents disappointment and unexpected expenses.

EgyptAir and Royal Air Maroc: Look Beyond the Obvious Hubs

Two other airlines worth investigating are EgyptAir and Royal Air Maroc.

EgyptAir provides transit accommodation in Cairo for certain qualifying international connections. Depending on the cabin, fare and connection, the minimum transit period may be six or eight hours, with accommodation generally limited to eligible connections of no more than 24 hours. It is also important that you either get the ‘ok to board’, which allows you to qualify for a visa on arrival from an accredited agent, or you can qualify for a visa on arrival with a UK, US, Schengen, or Canadian visa.

A traveller flying through Cairo could therefore investigate whether a qualifying connection provides an opportunity to experience Egypt before continuing to Europe or another destination.

Royal Air Maroc also provides transit assistance in Casablanca, including meals and, in certain circumstances, hotel accommodation subject to availability. For travellers connecting through Morocco to Europe, Casablanca could become more than an airport on the way to somewhere else. This is most possible for those with Morocco visas from the embassy in Abuja or those who qualify for E-visas (UK, US,Schengen,Canada etc visa).

However, neither airline’s transit accommodation policy should be mistaken for an unrestricted complimentary holiday. The rules depend on the ticket, connection and immigration requirements.

How to Actually Book a Stopover

Before purchasing your next international ticket, I suggest following a simple process.

First, identify the airline’s connecting hub. If you are flying Turkish Airlines, investigate Istanbul. If you are flying Qatar Airways, look at Doha. For Ethiopian Airlines, consider Addis Ababa.

Second, visit the airline’s official website and search for its stopover programme. Do not assume that selecting a long connection automatically qualifies you for complimentary accommodation.

Third, compare the ordinary return fare with an eligible stopover or multi-city itinerary. Check whether changing the connection increases the ticket price.

Fourth, confirm what the airline actually provides. Some programmes include a hotel and meals. Others offer discounted accommodation. Some provide tours, while others only assist with overnight transit.

Finally, check your visa eligibility before making any nonrefundable payments, and most importantly, if you’re not sure, speak to an IATA-accredited travel agent to guide you.

This final point is particularly important for Nigerian passport holders. A country may allow you to transit through its airport without a visa but require separate permission before you can leave the terminal.

The Real Savings Are in the Planning

Let us be clear: adding another destination is not automatically free. Even when an airline provides complimentary accommodation, you may still need to pay for visas, meals, transport and activities.

But compare that with purchasing an entirely separate international return ticket from Nigeria to visit the same country another time. You may find that a carefully planned stopover provides better overall value.

There is also the question of time. A 20-hour stopover does not mean 20 hours of sightseeing. Immigration, airport transfers, hotel check-in, and your next departure all reduce the time available. Sometimes a short guided tour is the sensible choice. Sometimes a full night or two allows you to enjoy the city properly.

And sometimes, the fastest connection is still the best option. The objective is not to complicate every journey. It is to understand the opportunities available before deciding.

Before You Book Your Next Flight

As we approach another year of travel, I want you to look differently at the international tickets you are considering. If you are travelling through Istanbul, Doha, Addis Ababa, Dubai, Cairo or Casablanca, ask what opportunities exist beyond the departure lounge.

Check the airline’s stopover conditions. Investigate its hotel arrangements. Compare the cost of extending your journey. And, most importantly, make sure you have the correct travel documents. You may discover that the airline taking you to your holiday destination can also introduce you to somewhere completely different.

Because sometimes, travelling more is not about buying another ticket; it is about discovering how much more you can do with the journey you are already taking.

item.content:encoded:
Chef Soliat Bada

Anyone who grew up in a Nigerian home knows the line. You suggest buying food outside, and before you finish the sentence, someone reminds you that there’s rice at home. It is usually the end of the conversation. In Asali Africa’s new series, it is where the conversation starts.

There’s Rice at Home is a cooking and conversation show from Asali Africa, the Lagos-based creative development agency, hosted by Chef Soliat Bada. In each episode, Soliat cooks one rice dish with a guest, and while the pot does its work, the two get into the kind of talk that usually happens around food: family, money and what success really looks like.

Rice is the most ordinary thing in a Nigerian kitchen, and the show makes a good case that it doesn’t have to taste ordinary. Over five episodes, released every two weeks, the menu travels from Jamaica to Saudi Arabia, back home to Nigeria and on to Louisiana.

You don’t just watch the food get made, either. The recipes are written up in full on Asali Africa’s website, with the ingredients and method laid out step by step, so you can watch Soliat cook a dish and then make it in your own kitchen.

The season opens with Rice and Peas with Oxtail, the Jamaican Sunday staple of rice cooked in coconut milk with red kidney beans (the “peas”), served beside rich, slow-cooked oxtail. Soliat’s guest is Michael Famoroti, co-founder of Stears, and their conversation turns to family and black tax: the expectation that once you start earning, you start supporting the people who raised you. Read the full recipe for Rice and Peas with Oxtail.

Rice and peas with oxtail, from Episode 1

Soliat Bada and Michael Famoroti in Episode 1

Episode 2 moves to the Gulf for lamb kabsa, Saudi Arabia’s national dish, fragrant with dried lime and seven spice. Soliat is joined by Bella Adeleke, CEO of Asali Africa and founder of the fashion label Garbe, for a conversation about redefining success. Read the full recipe for Lamb Kabsa.

Lamb kabsa, from Episode 2

Still to come are Nigerian fried rice with fried turkey and dodo, cooked with Toyin Jolapamo and Nneoma Mere; jambalaya with Goldie Iyamu and Vanessa Iloenyosi; and a season finale with Edwin Okolo and Temi Omolehinwa.

For more on Asali Africa and the products and ideas it develops, visit asali.africa.

item.content:encoded:
The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel.
It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes.

From Presence To Performance

That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point.

The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image.

The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be.

The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly.

Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled?

 Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation

TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth.

That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth.

Market scale does not, on its own, define technology leadership. What it does provide is evidence that a manufacturer has become an important participant in how the category develops. For a company operating at that scale, leadership increasingly includes helping make the technology easier to understand and giving consumers clearer ways to evaluate what they are buying.

Defining Category Leadership

Category leadership in Mini LED should therefore be broader than shipment rankings. It can be understood through four connected areas: sustained market scale, continued investment in the fundamentals of backlight performance, clearer performance criteria, and education that helps consumers distinguish between different implementations of the technology.

This is where the idea of good Mini LED becomes useful. It does not require creating a new certification or suggesting that every television should perform identically. It simply encourages a more complete discussion of the hardware and architecture that sit behind the Mini LED name.

Source references for internal verification:

  • • Omdia, Global TV shipments grow 3.6% in 2Q26 as market headwinds intensify, August 2026. Mini LED accounted for 13% of global TV shipments in Q2 2026.
  • • TCL Electronics 2026 Interim Results, citing Omdia global brand Mini LED TV shipment data for H1 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments, up 77.1% year on year, with shipment volume ranked No. 1 globally.
  • • TCL Electronics 2025 Annual Results, citing Omdia. TCL reported a 31.1% global Mini LED TV shipment share in 2025, ranked No. 1 globally, with shipments up 118.0% year on year.
